prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints in credit relationships amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B050, Kiyotaki and Moore, as a single-part, two-name prize. My alternatives have changed, and my confidence is a little firmer. The achievement is a dynamic mechanism in which borrowing is limited by collateral whose price is itself endogenous. A small shock to net worth then becomes a large and persistent fluctuation in credit, investment and output. The constraint comes from a financial-contracting enforcement problem, not from an ad hoc wedge, which makes it a disciplined foundation for macro-finance. It has had almost three decades to be extended, quantified and criticised. The chair's round-1 question asked what evidence targets the collateral channel and not financial frictions in general. My answer, from general knowledge and not independently verified, is that firm-level corporate-finance work tests the first-order channel: shocks to the value of pledgeable assets, such as land and real estate, move corporate investment and borrowing. Studies on Japanese land prices and on US real-estate shocks are examples. That supports the premise of the mechanism with firm-level data. The general-equilibrium amplification and propagation multiplier is much harder to identify directly, so the citation should rest on the mechanism and its influence, not on a claim that the multiplier has been measured. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: one originating paper, two authors, and a set that matches it exactly. I have not moved to B038 or B015. I have reconsidered both, but the common criteria I apply (a specific discovery, tested influence, attributable credit) still favour B050 slightly. This is a close judgement, and I would not oppose B038 on scientific grounds.
statement.case_against: Direct identification of the dynamic amplification channel remains weaker than the model's theoretical influence. Much of the confirming evidence supports the collateral channel at the firm level, but not the aggregate multiplier. The adjacent financial-accelerator lineage (Bernanke, Gertler, Gilchrist) is a different and more borrower-balance-sheet-based literature, and Bernanke is already a laureate for 2022. Even the two-name set is thematically close to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and some members may count that as overlap. My own profile lists me as an expert for that 2022 prize, so I may misjudge the distinctness either way. B050 has the narrowest explicit support of the leading candidates, and I treat that only as a signal that I have not shown the case to colleagues who rank it lower. Its policy footprint is narrower than B015's, and its empirical test record is thinner than B038's firm-level record. A committee that weights breadth of tested impact above attribution cleanliness could reasonably reverse my order.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B036 first with Autor, Hanson and Katz, and accepts Dorn for Katz as defensible. He asks me to say whether the collateral-constraint case, with Gertler and Gilchrist excluded, clears the attribution bar I apply to B036.
responses.response: I think it does. The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is one paper with two authors, and the credited set follows it exactly, so no one with a claim to the discovery is omitted. For B036 the set cannot match the discovery without choosing between two strands (task framework, trade-shock evidence), and Dorn's and Katz's claims point in opposite directions. I apply that standard to both: I do not hold B036's attribution against its scientific quality, only against how cleanly a three-name prize can reflect it. I accept that B050 compares badly on empirical record, since the amplification channel is harder to identify than local labour-market effects of import exposure. That is why B036 was a serious alternative in round 1. I have dropped it from my alternatives because the bundling problem you describe has no settled answer in this discussion.

responses.point: Enflo prefers B038 and answers my opening concern about the 2008 trade prize. She argues that 2008 covered scale economies, product differentiation and the location of production, while firm selection and reallocation are a different discovery, tested on microdata. She would word the citation around the mechanism, not the size of the welfare gains.
responses.response: This moved me. My opening ranked B038 eighth, mainly because I read it as overlapping with the 2008 recognition of new trade theory. Your distinction is persuasive: the unit of analysis, the testable predictions and the welfare channel are different. I also agree that the qualitative selection and reallocation result is better supported than any single gains-from-trade magnitude, so a mechanism-based citation is the right one. I have therefore moved B038 from last place to my first alternative. I do not put it first, for two reasons. The claims of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum remain a real attribution issue that your citation wording reduces but does not remove. I also see a trade-off between a cleaner credit set and a firmer empirical record, and I weight them about equally with B050's cleaner credit set.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B015 with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo, and finds the two-name B050 attribution argument clean. He ranks B015 higher because its influence on policy is more direct and more broadly confirmed than the collateral channel's, and invites colleagues to explain why B050 deserves a higher place.
responses.response: I accept the difference in breadth of policy influence, and I think it is real. My answer to your invitation is attribution and discovery definition. Your own case against B015 says that Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have arguably co-equal claims, that Calvo and Taylor predate the synthesis by two decades, and that the post-2021 episode is still contested. Those are the same costs the chair's questions ask all of us to price. B050 has none of the first two. On confirmation, I would not treat survival of a workhorse framework through 2008 and 2021-23 as confirming the specific building blocks credited to three people, which is Friberg's distinction and I agree with it. I keep B015 as an alternative and would not oppose it if the committee settles the citation and the trio.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B015 and finds the B050 case serious, with a clean two-name attribution B015 lacks. He accepts that a committee valuing clean attribution above breadth could reasonably reverse his ordering, and he asks whether Calvo or Gali is the better third name.
responses.response: I appreciate the concession, and I agree that this is the real choice: breadth and tested reach against attribution cleanliness. I do not think the evidence settles it. On the third name, I find your origin-versus-development reasoning for Calvo reasonable, but it shows how much the B015 trio depends on how the discovery is defined. For B050 I do not face that choice. One thing I would press is the 2022 overlap, which you also raise. I distinguish Kiyotaki-Moore from the banks and crises work of Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig by the mechanism: it concerns borrowers' collateral values and asset prices, not bank runs or the real effects of credit disruption in a banking system. I was an expert for that prize, so I flag that as a possible bias in how I draw that line.

responses.point: Dreber also prefers B050 with Kiyotaki and Moore, now with less confidence. She says the committee should not cite post-2008 evidence on financial frictions as validating this specific mechanism, and she wants evidence that targets the collateral channel itself.
responses.response: I agree with the standard and I have tried to apply it in my own case. Post-crisis evidence that credit frictions matter does not validate this mechanism. The relevant evidence is narrower: firm-level studies in which a change in the value of pledgeable assets shifts borrowing and investment. Those studies support the first-order channel. They do not establish the aggregate amplification multiplier, so I would word the citation around the mechanism and its influence on how fluctuations are modelled, and I would not assert that the multiplier has been measured. I think that leaves the case defensible, although we should say what it is not. My confidence is somewhat firmer than in round 1 because that evidence exists. It is not strong enough to call the case settled.

uncertainties: How much of the Kiyotaki-Moore amplification and propagation multiplier, as distinct from the first-order collateral channel, has been identified in data.

Whether the committee reads the collateral-constraint mechanism as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. I was an expert for that prize and may misjudge the line either way.

Whether the committee applies the same empirical-validation standard to theory-led candidates (B050, B021) and framework-level candidates (B015) as to microdata-based ones (B038, B036), and what that standard is.
Whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have claims strong enough that a Melitz-Helpman prize would be seen as incomplete, which affects how I rank B038 against B050.
How B015's attribution can be settled, and whether the post-2021 inflation episode counts for or against the credited building blocks.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files. I have not independently verified the scientific or credit record.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist is listed in my supplied profile, and none to the credited names on my alternatives B038 and B015. My field of corporate finance and financial contracting is intellectually adjacent to the enforcement friction behind B050, which could bias how I weigh it. I have long committee overlap with Hassler and Krusell, who prefer B015, and I treat their arguments as evidence only. Andersson discloses an SSE affiliation shared with me and other members. I also hold an adjunct post at Chicago Booth. The profile lists me among the KVA experts for the 2022 prize, so I may misjudge its overlap with B050. These are disclosures only and I have not adjudicated them.
